newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Market rally showers Deutsche with profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Market rally showers Deutsche with profits.

text.p: Shares in Deutsche Bank AG soared on Wednesday after the bank beat forecasts with a 27.5 percent jump in net income in the first half of 1997 as rallying financial markets showered it with profits.

Two days after Germany's banking sector was rocked by a mega-merger in Bavaria, the country's number-one bank called intense speculation of further tie-ups overdone and said it had no plans for acquisitions at home or in the U.S.
It was, however, considering an acquisition in the French banking sector provided the new Socialist-led government allows foreign banks to step into the market, Deutsche said.

This year's inexorable stock market rally and buoyant currency markets enabled Deutsche to chalk up record first-half trading profits and commission income which offset the negative impact of the weak mark on its costs, the bank said.
"It has rained porridge in the markets this year and we had the right spoon," a smiling Rolf Breuer told his first news briefing as chief executive since Hilmar Kopper retired in May.
The expansion of Deutsche's London-based investment banking business, though costly, had been an "overwhelming success" which was now bearing fruit.

Net income rose to 1.5 billion marks ($820 million) from 1.2 billion, beating analysts' forecasts which had averaged 1.36 billion marks. Earnings per share rose 26.1 percent to 2.90 marks from 2.30 marks.
The news helped push Deutsche's shares up as much as 11 percent to an all-time high of 134.30 marks. They later pared their gains to close floor trade at 126 marks.

The share price was also propelled by feverish investor interest in a sector brimming with merger speculation after Monday's news of a fusion between Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG (Hypo-Bank).
But Breuer said Deutsche saw no need to take any action in response to the Bavarian merger, which will create Germany's second largest bank and Europe's largest property financer.
While the banking world in Germany had changed, the competitive environment abroad, a key focus for Deutsche as an investment bank, was little changed.

"Our strategy is clearly different, we want to be a globally active investment bank and a focused universal bank. These aims have only been affected peripherally by the formation of a new number two in Germany."
Breuer said Deutsche was now so well positioned in its securities and asset management businesses that it was able to profit strongly from the rally in financial markets this year.
Pre-tax profit jumped 24 percent to 2.8 billion marks while operating profit after risk provisions rose 11.4 percent to 2.86 billion marks.
Profits were driven by trading income which jumped 48.3 percent rise to 2.0 billion marks, and by group net commission income which rose 25.7 percent to 4.1 billion marks.
Net interest income before risk provisions rose 7.1 percent to 5.7 billion marks, reflecting a sharp 12.4 percent rise in the balance sheet total to 996.1 billion marks since end-1996.
"We are confident that, if the markets remain favourable, we shall be able to achieve a higher profit for the whole of last year than 1997," Breuer said.
But the first-half results could not simply be multiplied by two to arrive at a full-year forecast, he added.

The income gains were overshadowed by a hefty 26.7 percent jump in administration costs, of which seven percentage points was explained by the mark's weakness against the dollar, the British pound and the yen.
The cost rise was also boosted by the adjustment of pension provisions, which had reduced the cost burden last year.

Stripping out those effects, costs grew 15 percent, reflecting the expansion of its investment banking as well as heavy spending on back office duties like settlement, risk controlling and documentation.
Deutsche said cost growth would slow down in the second half and that Deutsche had embarked on a savings drive with the aim of cutting costs by one billion marks by end-1998.
Analysts liked the earnings.

"It's a very good result, the figures were above expectations," said Christine Winkler, banking analyst at Bayerische Hypo-Bank who said she would probably raise her earnings forecast for the full year.
Risk provisions fell 35.3 percent to 500 million marks from 800 million marks, reflecting that corporate insolvencies are likely to have peaked.
Also, last year's risk provisions were boosted by funds set aside for engineering group KHD AG which Deutsche helped bail out.
